tools.change: Arithmetic checked: the four region weights and the seven area steps in the code match DermNet (a New Zealand dermatology reference). NOT sourced: the three bands the tool prints (mild / moderate / severe). DermNet gives no bands, and the funding criteria read (Pharmac) speak of a whole-body PASI "greater than 10" and use the DLQI beside it. Change: drop or re-source the bands; add the DLQI (licence first); also show the tool to the clinic dermatology role. SECOND PASS. (1) Formula: confirmed for the shared code by the United States second pass (weights, signs 0 to 4, area score 0 to 6, total 0 to 72). Two faults of the shared code found there apply here: a form with one box filled is scored as if every empty box were 0, and a score of 0 is called "Mild". (2) New Zealand, read on the Pharmac forms in force (secukinumab SA2624, etanercept SA2619): the whole-body criterion is a PASI "greater than 10"; Pharmac's consultation text of 2025 uses that figure under the heading of severe chronic plaque psoriasis. The tool calls 10 to 19.9 "Moderate". Example: a PASI of 12 reads "Moderate" on this screen and is above the funding limit. (3) The forms also have a route for the face, palm or sole (by the three sign sub-scores and the share of the area affected) and one for genital or flexural disease (by the DLQI); the tool has the whole-body score only. Renewal is written as a 75 per cent fall in the PASI or a DLQI improvement of 5 or more. Verdict unchanged: take the bands off, or let the country state them; add the DLQI only with its owner's licence.
tools.licence: unclear: a formula published in 1978; no owner's page was found (United States second pass). DLQI: needs permission from Cardiff University (read on the owner's page).

tools.change: RESULT WRONG FOR A CHILD UNDER 8. The code uses one set of region weights; DermNet gives different head-and-neck and lower-limb weights for ages 0 to 7. The tool says so only in its description and has no age field. Change: ask the age band and apply the published weights, or refuse under 8. The three bands are not sourced (DermNet gives none). Also show the tool to clinic dermatology. SECOND PASS. SAFETY, shared code (United States second pass, fault 3): the instrument's own user guide has a second set of region multipliers for children under 8; the tool never asks the age. Its example: a young child with severe eczema of the head and neck only is given 7.2 where the guide's multiplier gives 14.4. Ask the age, or refuse a patient under 8. BANDS, NEW ZEALAND: bpacnz's 2025 article on atopic dermatitis, which calls the EASI one of the most common scoring tools in New Zealand practice, gives moderate as 10 to 20 and severe as above 20; the tool calls 7 to 20.9 "Moderate" and 21 or above "Severe". Examples: an EASI of 20.5 reads "Moderate" here and is severe in the bpacnz article; an EASI of 8 reads "Moderate" here and is below the article's moderate range. The published strata read by the United States second pass are different again. FUNDING: Pharmac's form for upadacitinib (SA2599) asks for an EASI of 16 or more, or a DLQI of 10 or more, measured within the last month, and a 75 per cent fall for renewal. Half points, which the guide allows, cannot be entered. Verdict unchanged.

tools.change: SECOND PASS: unverified to revise. NO NEW ZEALAND GRADE TABLE WAS FOUND: three searches surfaced no page of the New Zealand Audiological Society that defines degrees of hearing loss. What New Zealand sources do use, read today: (1) the Hearing Aid Funding Scheme's eligibility criteria take the average of the THREE WORST thresholds among 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 kHz in the better ear and set their line at 56 dB HL, which they call moderately-severe or greater; (2) ACC does not grade by average at all: the 1999 regulations work out a percentage loss of hearing from eight frequencies with tables for the better and the worse ear, less an adjustment for age, the test done by an audiologist, and ACC accepts cover above a stated percentage. The tool averages all four frequencies and prints one of six grades. Example: thresholds of 30, 60, 60 and 60 dB give 52.5 dB and "Moderate hearing loss (41 to 55 dB)" on this screen, while the scheme's average of the three worst is 60 dB, above its line. From the United States second pass, for the shared code: the table of the paper the tool cites has a "slight" step from 16 to 25 dB that the tool folds into "Within normal limits", and the tool flags a difference between the ears at exactly 15 dB; ACC's guide speaks only of "a significant asymmetry" and gives no figure. Change: show the average without a grade until a New Zealand audiologist or otolaryngologist sets the grades; offer the scheme's three-worst average; show the tool to the audiologist role.

ACC's national concussion guidelines (updated January 2026) set six stages numbered 1 to 6 with minimum conditions: an earliest day for sport-specific training and a later earliest day for competition, counted from the injury. The tool has stages 0 to 5 with other names, no injury date and no minimum, so a doctor can record "full training and return to competition" with nothing recalling the national stand-down. It has six stages numbered 1 to 6; the count of days starts at the day of the injury (day 0); stage 5, sport-specific training, is at the earliest on day 14 and needs 14 days free of symptoms at rest; stage 6, competition, is "Earliest Day 21". Medical clearance before stages 5 and 6 is strongly recommended, not required. The guideline asks for slower progress in children, adolescents and female athletes, and sends elite sport to its own procedures. The tool has stages 0 to 5 under other names and holds no date. Two examples: (1) "Stage 5: full training and return to competition" can be recorded on day 3 and the screen does not object; (2) the numbers do not mean the same thing: stage 5 is competition in the tool and sport-specific training in the guideline, so a doctor who thinks in the guideline's numbers records a return to competition a stage early. tools.change: KEEP OFF until fixed. Confirmed against bpacnz: laboratories report the albumin-to-creatinine ratio in mg/mmol and the categories are cut at 3 and 30 mg/mmol. The kit converts to mg/g and cuts at 30 and 300, so a value from 3.0 to about 3.3 mg/mmol is placed one category too low, and so is a value from just above 30 to about 33.9. Second fault: the tool's "referral to a nephrologist" flags are not New Zealand's; bpacnz lists different criteria (a higher albuminuria figure, a rule for diabetes, a kidney-failure risk figure, and a lower threshold for Māori and Pacific patients and for younger patients). Change: classify in mg/mmol; take the referral prompts from the local source or drop them; show it to general practice. SECOND PASS. The bpacnz article was read again in full. (1) Categories: the ratio is in mg/mmol, cut at 3 and 30, one set for both sexes. With the kit's conversion a result of 3.0 mg/mmol becomes 26.5 mg/g and is called A1 where the article calls it microalbuminuria, and 31 mg/mmol is called A2 where the article calls it macroalbuminuria; the kit's two boundaries fall at about 3.4 and 33.9 mg/mmol. (2) Referral: the article lists an eGFR below 30; persistent macroalbuminuria; diabetes with an eGFR below 45; a fall in eGFR stated two ways (a percentage between two measurements, and an amount within twelve months when the starting eGFR is below 60); a five-year risk of kidney failure of "≥ 3 – 5%"; haematuria; resistant hypertension; and a lower threshold for younger patients and for Māori and Pacific peoples (reported as the source states it). The tool's four flags are an eGFR below 30, the kit's A3, a fall of more than a quarter in a year, and "the very-high-risk cell". Two examples: a patient with diabetes, an eGFR of 40 and a normal ratio gets no flag from the tool and meets a criterion of the article; a ratio of 31 mg/mmol that persists, with an eGFR of 70, gets no flag and meets another. (3) Two faults of the shared code confirmed by the United States second pass apply on the day this is switched on: a risk colour is shown when no urine result was typed (an eGFR of 75 alone reads "low risk"), and the flags are labelled as KDIGO criteria but are not KDIGO's list. kitGaps: A country cannot change WHO SEES a tool of the shared English set: the roles sit on the shared text (countries/_dil/en/araclar/*.ts, HamArac.roller). A pack can only switch a tool off (araclar.kapali) or reword it (araclar.degisen).
A country cannot add, drop or re-divide a role: all five English packs take the same 40 keys (EN_ROLLER), and lib/ulke/rolEslemesi.test.ts requires exactly forty.

A country cannot bring a tool of its own: every mechanism must be in the kit catalogue shared by all countries, and the tool texts and slots are the shared set's. EnAraclarGirdisi has no place for a country's own tools or own slots (beyond tools it closes).
New Zealand state-system tools (ACC, Work and Income, Pharmac) need an "nz" list in countries/yasak-araclar.json so that wall rule D7 keeps them out of every other country.
Thresholds are applied only in the kit's own unit after conversion (albumin-to-creatinine ratio in mg/g). A country whose published limits are in another unit (mg/mmol) cannot state them.
HbA1c has no unit choice (lab-izlem refuses values outside 3 to 20); LabOlcusu has no entry for it.
A pack's numbers (parametreler) are compared in the kit's unit, with nothing saying so: haemoglobin limits would have to be typed in g/dL in a country that reports g/L.
The options of a choice field are fixed in the kit (report categories, return-to-sport stages): a country cannot supply its own list.
Dose arithmetic has one unit (mg per kg): no micrograms, no units.
The citation shown under a result (kaynak) is fixed in the kit: a country cannot show its national source.
The patient file has no ethnicity and no deprivation quintile, both inputs of the national cardiovascular equations (the earlier audit, finding C8, already notes ethnicity).
A slot records what is missing and who supplies it, but not a licence status: there is no field to hold "permission asked / granted / refused" per tool per country.
